title: user-sim-sprint-notes-priyanka-2028-06
content:
Sprint scratchpad: lightweight user simulators + latency-aware evals

Goals (what I want by EOW):
- Prototype a tiny on-device user simulator that emits session-level requests with realistic think-time distributions and retrieval patterns.
- Add latency-aware metrics to the eval harness: time-to-first-byte, TTF-T (time-to-first-token), P50/P95/P99 token latency, request tail vs queued batches.
- Run 3 scaled runs against hosted and a small private-node (8xA100-ish sim) to capture behavior differences and variability.

Background / motivation:
- Our current evals treat latency as an average token/sec number. That hides burstiness and queueing behavior that breaks customer SLAs.
- Prod traffic is bursty: short chat sessions (2-6 turns) + occasional long context (>8k tokens) retrievals. We need end-to-end sims to expose catastrophic tails when batching and caching interact.
- User simulators used in dialog research (see linked arXiv) can be adapted: keep it simple (Markov-turn model, retrieval-trigger prob).

Design sketch for the simulator:
- Session model: each session = N turns (sampled from empirical distro: {1: 0.35, 2:0.28, 3:0.2, 4+:0.17})
- Turn think time: mixture distribution (exp for quick, lognormal for distracted longer delays). Fit params from product telemetry later.
- Query types: {short-completion, chat-turn, retrieval-augmented, rerank} with sampling weights tunable per scenario.
- Retrieval pattern: for RAG turns, simulate 1..k retrievers, add retrieval latency (sampled) and sim partial hits (to test effective prefix caching)
- Failure injection: configurable p(error) on model node, network timeouts, and sudden capacity drop (simulate noisy neighbor)

Why this reveals tail behavior:
- Continuous batching + autoscaling policies can create build-up during bursts; TTF-T for first token increases dramatically for small latencies if batches wait to fill.
- KV/prefix caching helps when same session repeats; but cross-session cache warmup is different: long-tail contexts cause high memory pressure and eviction which shows up as degradation in P99.

Metrics to capture (added to harness):
- Core: request_count, success_rate, avg_latency, p50/p95/p99 latency (request-level and token-level)
- Session-aware: avg_turn_latency, session_completion_time, first_turn_latency
- Batch metrics: batch_size_distribution, wait_time_before_dispatch
- Cache metrics: cache_hit_rate_by_session_age, avg_kv_load_time
- Cost proxies: tokens_generated_per_second, gpu_utilization_samples, effective_tokens_per_gpu_hour

Quick experiments to run this week:
1) Baseline: 1000 concurrent sessions, mix=default, run hosted vs small private cluster. Collect 30m trace.
2) Burst test: step to 5x load over 30s, hold 2m, observe queue growth and TTF-T degradation.
3) Long-context stress: 10% of sessions include 12k context (simulate chunking/streaming). Measure memory spill / latency impact.

Data collection plan:
- Instrumented trace events per request: session_id, turn_idx, request_type, batch_id, model_variant, queued_ms, dispatch_ms, first_token_ms, last_token_ms, token_count, success_flag
- Export to S3 for offline analysis (parquet) and quick realtime dashboards for p95/p99 using existing console hooks.

Implementation notes / snippets:
- Small python harness skeleton (pseudo):
  - async loop spawn sessions, each session awaits random think time, then emits request payload (type + context id).
  - use aiohttp to POST to endpoint, measure timing with monotonic time.
  - support headers to route to different model variants / regions.
- For retrieval sim: reuse local sqlite mini-index to return fake doc ids and simulated retrieval latencies. Keeps cost low.

Open questions / risks:
- How to pick think-time distribution seeds to match real customers? We need a quick telemetry pull from prod; ask SWE telemetry team for 2 weeks of anonymized session event times. RI-1428 filed.
- Should simulator model user edits (prompt refinement) vs new queries? For now keep binary: revised vs next-turn.
- Streaming semantics: TTF-T measurement depends on token chunking at runtime; need clarity on token flush thresholds in serving runtime (talk to runtime eng).

Immediate TODOs:
- [ ] Wire up basic harness prototype (Priyanka) — target: end of day 6/13
- [ ] Request sample session telemetry export (Owen) — blocked on data access; see RI-1428
- [ ] Add batch wait_time metric to console traces (Evelyn) — ask observability for quick metric map
- [ ] Create a lightweight dashboard (p99-focused) for the two comparison runs

Notes-to-self / heuristics discovered while thinking:
- For SLA-like tests, measure both absolute p99 and delta p99 when comparing variants; a small absolute change can be critical if it crosses SLA thresholds.
- When simulating cache warmup, run two-phase test: cold start 10m then steady-state 40m to see asymptotic hit-rate.
- Use tiny synthetic prompt families rather than fully realistic prompts for early perf tests; this isolates runtime behavior from model quality fuzz.

References and reading (quick skim log):
- simulated users for dialog evaluation (paper - arXiv) -> linked_artifacts[0]
- internal PR: user-sim harness (proto) -> linked_artifacts[1]
- jira: RI-1428 (telemetry export) -> linked_artifacts[2]
- Confluence: latency-aware-evals doc -> linked_artifacts[3]

After-action plan (if prototype shows large tails):
- Immediate: change autoscale policy to prefer smaller max batch wait_time for SLO-sensitive routes; include canary.
- Medium-term: integrate session-aware routing so sessions with short think-times get priority lanes (low-batch-wait); evaluate cost impact.
- Long-term: build a 'session cache' to keep KV for hot sessions pinned in memory for a short TTL to reduce evictions.

End notes: This is a working doc — messy by design. Next iteration will fold in telemetry histograms and a simple Jupyter report with p95/P99 plots. If Owen or Evelyn have other ideas ping me in #eng-evals or leave comments in linked PR.

-- Priyanka
